segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, has found?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about—but not before God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For what does the scripture say?

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now when someone works, the wages are not counted as a matter of grace but as a matter of debt.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when someone does not work but believes in the one who justifies the ungodly, that person’s faith is counted as righteousness,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as David also pronounces the blessing on the person to whom God counts righteousness apart from works:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered;

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Is this blessing, then, on the circumcised, or on the uncircumcised as well? For we say,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: How then was it counted? When he was circumcised or when he was uncircumcised? Not when he was circumcised, but when he was uncircumcised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while uncircumcised, so that he would be the father of all who believe while uncircumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the father of the circumcised, for those who are not only circumcised but also follow in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while uncircumcised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the promise to Abraham or to his offspring, that he would be heir of the world, did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise nullified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the law brings about wrath; but where there is no law, there is no transgression either.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is why it is by faith, so that it may be a matter of grace, so that the promise may be guaranteed to all the offspring—not only to those who are of the law but also to those who are of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as it is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I have made you a father of many nations.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He is our father in the sight of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls things that are not as though they were.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Against hope, in hope, he believed, so that he became the father of many nations, according to what had been said:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “So shall your offspring be.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And without weakening in faith he considered his own body, as good as dead since he was about a hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah’s womb;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: yet with regard to God’s promise he did not waver through lack of faith, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and being fully convinced that what God had promised he was also able to do.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is why

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “it was counted to him as righteousness.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the words

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “it was counted to him”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: were not written for his sake alone,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but also for ours. It is going to be counted to us who believe in the one who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who was handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification.

notes.traditional: What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, has found?
notes.note: The sentence can be punctuated differently: 'What then shall we say? Have we found Abraham to be our forefather according to the flesh?', which would make the question about whether Abraham's fatherhood is merely a matter of physical descent. The manuscripts also vary in where they place 'found', and a few omit it. The rendering here follows the majority of translations and commentators.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: 'justify', 'justification', 'righteous' and 'righteousness' in this chapter all translate forms of the same root. To justify someone is to declare or set them in the right, and the reader should hear the link with 'righteousness' in verse 3. Translations into most other languages use one word for 'justice' throughout, and some scholars prefer 'justice' in English as well.

The verb is an ordinary bookkeeping term for entering something to a person's account, which is why Paul can move straight to wages and debt in verse 4. The quotation is Genesis 15:6 in its Greek form, and the same verb recurs in the psalm quoted in verses 7–8 (Psalm 32:1–2). It is rendered 'count' throughout the chapter so that the eleven occurrences can be heard as one word.

In everyday Greek the word meant a favour freely given, and many modern versions translate 'as a gift' here. 'Grace' is kept because Paul uses the identical phrase again in verse 16, and the argument depends on the reader hearing the two together.

To a reader who knew the Scriptures this phrase was startling. In the Greek Old Testament acquitting the ungodly is what a corrupt judge does, and it is forbidden (Exodus 23:7; Proverbs 17:15; Isaiah 5:23). Paul deliberately describes God in the terms of that prohibition.

notes.phrase: not only circumcised but also follow
notes.traditional: not only circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps
notes.note: The Greek repeats the article before 'follow', which strictly would describe two groups: the circumcised, and also those who follow Abraham's faith. Most interpreters judge that the argument requires one group, circumcised people who also share Abraham's faith, and treat the extra article as loose grammar or an early slip. The rendering here follows that view.

Genesis promises Abraham a particular land and many descendants; it never says in so many words that he would inherit the world. By Paul's time Jewish interpretation had widened the land promise to take in the whole earth, and Paul assumes that reading.

The Greek word translated 'nations' here, quoting Genesis 17:5, is the same word translated 'Gentiles' elsewhere in Romans (for example 3:29). Paul's point depends on this: the scripture that made Abraham father of many nations is, to a Greek ear, also making him father of many Gentiles.

notes.phrase: calls things that are not as though they were
notes.traditional: calleth those things which be not as though they were
notes.note: The phrase can mean that God summons non-existent things into existence, the language of creation, as several modern versions translate it. It can also mean that God speaks of things that do not yet exist, such as Abraham's descendants, as if they already did. The rendering here keeps the Greek wording, which allows both.

notes.traditional: he considered not his own body
notes.note: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read 'he did not consider his own body'. The earliest witnesses lack the negative, and that is the text translated here: Abraham looked squarely at the facts and still believed. Either reading makes the same overall point.

notes.traditional: delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification
notes.note: The same Greek preposition stands in both halves of the verse, and 'for' is used twice to keep the parallel. In the first half it means 'because of'. In the second it is usually taken as 'with a view to' our justification, though some read 'because of' there too. 'Handed over' echoes the Greek of Isaiah 53:12, where the servant is handed over because of the people's sins.

Seed, offspring and descendants are all in use, and Galatians 3:16 turns on the word being singular, so the choice must hold across Romans, Galatians, Hebrews and the Gospels.
Ranges over grace, favour, gift and thanks; the line between the theological term and the everyday sense needs a single policy.
Paul's uses run from physical descent to human nature opposed to the Spirit; translations diverge widely (flesh, human nature, sinful nature, natural descent) and readers need consistency.
A favourite Pauline verb rendered variously as nullify, abolish, make void, destroy and bring to nothing; it links Romans 3:31, 4:14, 6:6 and 7:2–6 and many other passages.
